mcqs.question: Four different pairs of forces are applied about the same pivot. Which pair will produce torques that act in opposite directions about the pivot?

options.A: Force of 10 N upward applied 0.3 m to the right of the pivot and another force of 10 N upward applied 0.3 m to the left of the pivot.
options.B: Force of 10 N upward applied 0.3 m to the right of the pivot and a force of 10 N downward applied at the same point (0.3 m to the right).
options.C: Force of 10 N to the right applied 0.3 m above the pivot and a force of 10 N to the left applied at the same height.
options.D: Two identical forces of 10 N upward both applied 0.3 m to the right of the pivot.

mcqs.answer: Force of 10 N upward applied 0.3 m to the right of the pivot and a force of 10 N downward applied at the same point (0.3 m to the right).
mcqs.explanation: Torque is given by τ = r × F. For the pair in option B the forces are opposite in direction while acting at the same lever arm, so their torques have equal magnitude but opposite sense (one out of the page, the other into the page). The other options either give torques in the same sense or zero torque. Hence option B correctly yields opposite‑direction torques.

mcqs.question: A uniform beam 2 m long is pivoted 0.5 m from its left end. The beam’s weight (20 N) acts at its centre. A 30 N weight hangs 0.2 m to the left of the pivot. What upward force must be applied at the right end (0.5 m to the right of the pivot) to keep the beam in rotational equilibrium?
mcqs.explanation: Take anticlockwise torques as positive. Torque due to the 30 N weight: 30 N × 0.2 m = 6 N·m (counter‑clockwise). Torque due to the beam’s weight: 20 N × 0.5 m = 10 N·m (clockwise). Let the required upward force be F. Its torque: F × 0.5 m (counter‑clockwise). Setting Στ = 0: 6 + 0.5F = 10 ⇒ 0.5F = 4 ⇒ F = 8 N upward. Option B is correct.

mcqs.question: Which of the following statements correctly defines torque?

options.A: Torque is a measure of the tendency of a force to cause linear acceleration.
options.B: Torque is a vector quantity equal to the cross product of the position vector and the force vector.
options.C: Torque is the product of mass and acceleration.
options.D: Torque is the scalar magnitude of a force.

mcqs.answer: Torque is a vector quantity equal to the cross product of the position vector and the force vector.
mcqs.explanation: Torque (τ) is defined as τ = r × F, the cross product of the radius (position) vector r from the axis to the point of application and the force vector F. This makes torque a vector whose direction follows the right‑hand rule. Options A, C, and D describe other concepts (linear force, Newton’s second law, and force magnitude).

mcqs.question: A force of 15 N acts perpendicular to a lever at a distance of 0.4 m from the pivot. What is the magnitude of the moment of this force?
mcqs.explanation: Moment (torque) magnitude is given by τ = F × r when the force is perpendicular to the lever. Here τ = 15 N × 0.4 m = 6 N·m. The other options arise from arithmetic errors.

mcqs.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes the lever arm from the line of action of a force?

options.A: The lever arm is the perpendicular distance from the axis to the line of action; the line of action is the straight line along which the force acts.
options.B: The lever arm is the length of the force vector; the line of action is the point where the force is applied.
options.C: The lever arm and the line of action are two names for torque and moment, respectively.
options.D: The lever arm is measured along the direction of the force, while the line of action is measured perpendicular to it.

mcqs.answer: The lever arm is the perpendicular distance from the axis to the line of action; the line of action is the straight line along which the force acts.
mcqs.explanation: The lever arm (also called moment arm) is defined as the shortest (perpendicular) distance between the axis of rotation and the line of action of the force. The line of action itself is the infinite line extending in the direction of the force. Options B, C, and D misstate these definitions.

mcqs.question: A horizontal force of 20 N is applied at the free end of a 0.5 m long rod that is pivoted at the other end. The force is directed along the length of the rod (to the right). What is the direction of the torque about the pivot?

options.D: Both into and out of the page

mcqs.explanation: Torque τ = r × F. Here the force acts along the line joining the pivot and the point of application, so the position vector r and force vector F are collinear. The cross product of parallel (or antiparallel) vectors is zero, giving no torque. Hence option C is correct; the other options assume a non‑zero lever arm.

mcqs.question: A seesaw is balanced on a central pivot. A child of weight 40 N sits 1.2 m to the left of the pivot. At what distance from the pivot must a child of weight 30 N sit on the right side to keep the seesaw in equilibrium?
mcqs.explanation: For rotational equilibrium, clockwise torque = anticlockwise torque. Left torque: 40 N × 1.2 m = 48 N·m. Let d be the distance for the 30 N child on the right: 30 N × d = 48 N·m ⇒ d = 48/30 = 1.6 m. Option C matches this value.

mcqs.question: When opening a door, a force is applied at the handle 0.8 m from the hinges. Which of the following best defines the torque produced by this action?

options.A: Torque is the product of the force applied and the distance from the hinge measured along the line of action.
options.B: Torque is a scalar quantity that causes linear motion of the door.
options.C: Torque is a vector quantity equal to the cross product of the position vector from the hinge to the point of application and the applied force.
options.D: Torque is the same as the work done by the force while the door rotates.

mcqs.answer: Torque is a vector quantity equal to the cross product of the position vector from the hinge to the point of application and the applied force.
mcqs.explanation: The torque about the hinges is τ = r × F, where r is the vector from the hinge to the handle (0.8 m) and F is the applied force. This definition captures both magnitude (F r sinθ) and direction (given by the right‑hand rule). Option A omits the perpendicular component, B confuses torque with linear force, and D confuses torque with work.
